Abstract—This paper addresses t he static voltage stability 
constraints and complex coupling relationships in multi -
voltage-level transmission sections for large -scale renewable 
energy integration systems . The study extracts two typica l 
topological structures —parallel coupling and series  coupling 
sections—from ac tual grid features and analyz es their 
interactive mechanisms affecting static voltage stability  limits. 
Research reveals that  in parallel systems, power flow 
distribution significantly impacts the overall transmission limit, 
with optimal limits achieved when heavily loaded branches 
concentrate on low -impedance paths . In series systems, the 
contribution of proximal station power growth to total 
transmission capacity exhibits nonli near variation (sensitivity 
decreases with increasing output). Validated through actual 
grid simulations, the sensitivity of key node power flow to 
section limits is quantified, demonstrating that uniform power 
verification may cause conservatism or securi ty risks. The 
findings provide theoretical support for online ass essment of 
multi-level transmission  section limit and active power 
optimization control, enhancing utilization rates while ensuring 
security to promote renewable energy accommodation. 
Keywords—renewable energy, static voltage stability , multi-
voltage-level transmission sections 
I. INTRODUCTION  
Due to the uneven distribution of resources, renewable 
energy bases are often geographically distant from load 
centers in many cases, making direct power supply to end -
users challenging. Consequently, it is necessary to connect 
energy bases with load centers through multi -voltage-level 
high-voltage transmission lines and substations to achieve 
long-distance power transmission and dispatch. With the 
increasing scale of renewable energy installations and the 
growing hierarchy of power aggregation, the scenario of 
delivering renewable energy through multi -voltage-level 
transmission sections has become increasingly preval ent [1-
2]. In such delivery systems, volt age security issues emerge 
as critical constraints limiting the power transfer capacity of 
transmission sections at all levels, primarily due to the 
absence of conventional power support and the extended 
electrical distance of renewable energy delivery corridors [3]. 
In practical operations, voltage security verification is 
predominantly incorporated into renewable energy 
operational limit assessments through offline calculations. 
Among these, static voltage stability constraints constitute 
one of the prima ry operational limitations for renewable 
energy-integrated grids  [4]. Taking China's Jibei regional 
power grids as an example, static voltage stability constraints 
serve as decisive factors in determining power transfer limits 
for certain renewable energ y delivery sections. Analytical 
methods for static voltage stability problems mainly include 
the continuation power flow method  [5], Jacobian matrix 
singularity method [6], and sensitivity analysis method [7]. 
The PV curve provides an intuitive understanding  of static 
voltage stability by illustrating how system voltage varies 
and potentially collapses as wind power active output 
increases. Ref [8] demonstrates that as system operation 
approaches static voltage stability limits, voltage fluctuations 
caused by  equivalent wind power active power variations 
become significantly amplified. 
Static voltage stability exhibits strong coupling with 
power flow distribution across transmission sections. This 
results in varying static voltage stability characteristics 
among different voltage -level transmission sections within 
the same region as their power flow distributions change. 
Existing voltage security risk assessment methods, which 
assume uniform renewable energy generation across all 
sections, can only evaluate static voltage security risks under 
typical operating conditions. Such approaches may yield 
overly conservative limits that underutilize transmission 
capacity or produce optimistic estimates that jeopardize 
system operational security [9]. 
This paper conducts the analysis of static voltage stability 
in large -scale renewable energy delivery systems through 
multi-level transmission sections. First, by examining the 
topological characteristics of multi -voltage-level 
transmission networks, typical section couplin g types are 
identified, with mechanistic analysis performed on the 
coupling relationships of transmission limits for each type. 
Case studies based on actual grid simulations are developed, 
employing sensitivity analysis to quantify the contributions 
of key node power flow states to section transfer capacity.

II. THE STATIC VOLTAGE STABILITY LIMIT OF THE 
RENEWABLE ENERGY TRANSMISSION SYSTEM 
The P -V curve method, as an effective approach for 
studying voltage stability issues in power systems, can 
indicate the cr itical voltage and limit power of load nodes, 
and provide corresponding voltage margin and active power 
margin, thus being widely applied. It establishes a 
relationship curve between the node voltage and the power 
flow of a regional load or transmission ch annel, thereby 
indicating the degree to which the regional load level or 
transmission channel power level causes the entire system to 
approach voltage collapse. 
When applying the P -V curve method to analyze the 
static voltage stability of power grids with renewable energy 
integration, since the impact of renewable energy power 
injection on voltage stability needs to be considered, P 
represents the active power generated by new energy sources, 
while V can refer to the terminal voltage of generators, the 
point-of-common-coupling (PCC) voltage, or the voltage at 
other critical nodes in the collection system. 
Due to the low -voltage ride-through (LVRT) strategies 
adopted by renewable energy systems, their transmission 
systems do not experience voltage instability  in the 
traditional sense [8]. However, when the system approaches 
the inflection point of its P -V curve, active power 
fluctuations will cause significant voltage variations, which 
are detrimental to system operation. As shown in Fig.1, for a 
renewable energy transmission system in a certain region, 
when the transmitted power approaches the static voltage 
stability limit, the amplitude of voltage fluctuations caused 
by the same active power change increases significantly. 
Therefore, in actual operation, a ma rgin is typically applied 
to the theoretical inflection point of the P -V curve to 
determine the practical static voltage stability limit for new 
energy transmission, as illustrated in Fig.2.

B. The Simulation results of Static Voltage Stability Limit 
The complex section coupling relationship makes the 
power transfer capability of the section highly affected by the 
regional active power flow distribution. Take the static 
voltage stability limit of a secondary section's power sending 
area as an example. The limit of Section A refers to the 
renewable energy power transfer limit connected to the 
500kV substation, while the limit of Section B is the static 
voltage stability limit of the 220kV gathering station's 
outgoing lines. Section B is connected to Section A via 
220kV transmission lines, and there are also renewable 
energy stations directly connected to Section A through 
220kV lines. 
Simulation results show that the calculation results of 
section power transfer limits vary significantly under 
different power flow conditions. As shown in Fig.4, when all 
renewable energy stations in the area output power uniformly, 
the power transfer limit of Section A is relatively large, while 
the limit of downstream Section B is relatively small. 
Increasing the active power transfer level of Section B can 
indeed improve its own limit, but the power transfer limit of 
Section A decreases rapidly, leading to a reduction in the 
overall regional limit. 
 
Fig. 4. Static voltage stability limits in a secondary section's  power 
sending area  under different power flow conditions (1-Uniform 
Output, 2-Only Section B has power output ; 3- Section B has power 
output of 800MW, Section A has power output of 1125MW) 
IV. ANALYSIS OF STATIC VOLTAGE STABILITY LIMIT FOR 
DIFFERENT SECTION COUPLING TYPES 
A. Analysis of Section Coupling Types 
By simplifying and extracting typical section coupling 
types, they can be summarized as parallel coupling 
transmission systems and series coupling transmission 
systems, as shown in Fig.5 and Fig.6. In the parallel coupling 
transmission system of Fig.5, two renewable energy stations 
are connected in parallel to an infinite bus through their 
respective transmission lines. In the series coupling 
transmission system of Fig .6, the remote renewable energy 
station is connected to the proximal station via a transmission 
line, and then transmitted to the infinite bus.

Fig.8 shows the sensitivity simulation results of the 
power changes in the proximal station of an actual   
secondary section's power sending area  in Jibei power grids  
to the section transmission limit. It can be seen that as the 
power of the proximal station gradually increases, its 
sensitivity to the section transmission limit shows a gradual 
decreasing tr end. When the active power of the proximal 
station is close to zero, its sensitivity to the total renewable 
energy transmission limit of the region is close to 1, meaning 
that its active power growth hardly causes the transmission 
limit of the remote section to decrease, and the active power 
growth of the proximal station can significantly improve the 
total transmission capacity. When the active power level of 
the proximal station is below 900 MW, with the increase of 
its active power, its sensitivity to the total transmission limit 
decreases slowly. That is, the same active power growth of 
the proximal station leads to a larger decre ase in the 
transmission limit of the remote section. When the active 
power level of the proximal station exceeds 900 MW, its 
sensitivity to the total transmission limit decreases rapidly. 
At this time, increasing the active power of the proximal 
station will significantly reduce the transmission limit of the 
remote section, and its positive contribution to the total 
transmission limit becomes smaller and smaller.

V. CONCLUSION 
This paper studies the static voltage stability issues of 
renewable energy through multi -voltage-level section 
transmission systems faced by ac tual power grids. The 
complex section coupling problem is decomposed into a 
series coupling transmission system and a parallel coupling 
transmission system. A complementary approach combining 
simplified model analytical analysis and actual system 
simulation results is adopted to investigate the interactive 
influence laws of power limits of each coupling section 
under static voltage stability constraints. The study shows 
that the power flow distribution of different -level sections 
and different power flow gr owth patterns between sections 
have obvious regular influences on th e overall renewable 
energy transmission capacity of the region. The research 
findings can provide a theoretical basis for the online 
assessment of tr ansmission limits in multi -voltage-level 
section transmission systems. On the premise of ensuring 
safety, from the perspective of fully releasing the 
transmission capacity of sections, it is conducive to 
promoting renewable energy consumption.
